problem: Implement a cache where each entry automatically expires after a configurable time-to-live (TTL) — a `Get` for an expired key should behave as a miss, even if nothing has proactively cleaned it up yet.
solution:
Store each entry alongside an absolute expiry timestamp (`DateTime.UtcNow + ttl`) computed at insert time, rather than a "time remaining" value that would need to be actively counted down. On every `Get`, compare the stored expiry to the current time: if it's passed, treat it as a miss and evict the entry right there (lazy/on-access expiration) rather than returning stale data.

Lazy expiration alone means memory for expired-but-never-accessed-again entries is never reclaimed; a production version typically pairs it with a periodic background sweep that removes expired entries proactively. Use `ConcurrentDictionary` rather than `Dictionary` plus a lock if the cache needs to be safe under concurrent access, which most cache use cases do.

Time: O(1) for `Set` and `Get`. Space: O(number of live entries) — bounded by TTL and write rate, not by how long the process has been running.
scenario: A feature-flag service used exactly this lazy-expiration TTL cache to avoid re-fetching flag values from a remote config service on every request, while still guaranteeing a flag change took effect within its TTL window instead of being cached indefinitely.

problem: Implement a minimal dependency-injection container: `Register<TService, TImplementation>()` records a mapping, and `Resolve<T>()` returns an instance, automatically constructing and injecting any constructor-parameter dependencies recursively — a tiny version of what ASP.NET Core's built-in container does.
solution:
The core trick is recursion through reflection: to build an instance of a type, look at its constructor's parameter types, resolve each of those (recursively — a dependency can itself have dependencies), then call `Activator.CreateInstance` with the resolved arguments. The registration dictionary just maps an interface type to the concrete type that should be constructed when that interface is requested; if a type isn't registered, resolve it directly as itself (useful for concrete classes with no interface).

This version deliberately leaves out two things real containers add on top of the same core idea: lifetime management (everything here is effectively transient — a new instance every `Resolve` call, with no singleton/scoped concept) and circular-dependency detection (two types depending on each other recursively would stack-overflow here rather than fail with a clear error). Worth naming both explicitly if asked "what would you add for production use."

Time: O(depth of the dependency graph) per `Resolve`, each level doing reflection work that's more expensive than a normal method call — real containers cache the resolved constructor/plan per type to avoid re-reflecting on every call. Space: O(depth of the dependency graph) for the recursion.
scenario: A plugin-based application used a minimal reflection-based container much like this one to auto-wire a plugin's declared dependencies at load time, and explicitly punted on circular-dependency detection — exactly as this exercise flags — until a real plugin pair with a circular reference caused a stack overflow in production.

problem: Implement a minimal middleware pipeline, similar in spirit to ASP.NET Core's: middleware components are registered in order, each can run code before and after calling the next component in the chain, and any component can short-circuit the pipeline by simply not calling `next`.
solution:
Model each middleware as a function that wraps the next delegate in the chain: `Func<RequestDelegate, RequestDelegate>`. Building the pipeline means composing these wrappers — and the order you fold them in matters: fold from the *last* registered middleware to the *first*, so that the first middleware registered ends up as the outermost wrapper. That's what makes each middleware's "before" code run in registration order and its "after" code (anything after its call to `next`) run in the reverse order — exactly how ASP.NET Core's pipeline behaves.

Short-circuiting falls out naturally from the design: a middleware that never calls `next()` simply stops the chain there — nothing downstream runs, and control unwinds back through only the "after" portions of the middlewares that already ran.

Time: O(1) overhead per middleware per request (a delegate call), so O(n) total for n middleware components. Space: O(n) for the composed delegate chain.
scenario: An internal API framework built at a fintech company used exactly this middleware-composition pattern for auth, logging, and rate-limiting layers, and a security review specifically checked that an auth middleware which didn't call `next()` correctly short-circuited the pipeline instead of letting a request leak through to the handler.

problem: Implement a reusable pagination helper for an API: given an `IQueryable<T>` (e.g. an EF Core `DbSet`), a page number, and a page size, return both the requested page of items and metadata (total count, total pages) — without pulling the whole table into memory to count it.
solution:
The trap here is calling `.ToList()` (or otherwise enumerating) before counting — that would materialize every row into memory just to get a count. Stay in `IQueryable<T>` for both operations: call `.Count()` on the query before applying `.Skip`/`.Take`, and it gets translated into a `SELECT COUNT(*)` at the database rather than an in-memory count. Then apply `.Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize).Take(pageSize)` and only *that* call to `.ToList()` executes a query, pulling back just the one page's worth of rows.

Wrapping this as an extension method on `IQueryable<T>` keeps calling code simple (`dbContext.Orders.Where(...).ToPagedResult(page, pageSize)`) while leaving the actual query composition — filtering, sorting — entirely up to the caller before pagination is applied.

Time: O(log n) or O(n) for the count and the page fetch depending on the database's indexing (not a concern of the C# code itself, but worth mentioning that an unindexed `COUNT(*)` on a huge table isn't free). Space: O(page size) in application memory, regardless of total row count.
scenario: An admin dashboard team hit a production incident when an early version of a list endpoint called `.ToList()` before counting, pulling a million-row table into memory just to report its count; rewriting it to keep everything in `IQueryable<T>` until `.Skip`/`.Take` fixed both the memory spike and the response time.

problem: Implement a function that parses one line of CSV into its fields, correctly handling fields wrapped in double quotes that contain commas, and escaped double-quotes (`""`) inside a quoted field representing a single literal `"`. Explain why `line.Split(',')` is the wrong first instinct.
solution:
A plain `Split(',')` breaks the moment any field contains a comma inside quotes (e.g. `"Smith, John",42` should be two fields, not three) — CSV isn't actually comma-delimited in the naive sense, it's comma-delimited *outside of quoted regions*. That requires tracking state as you scan character by character rather than delimiting blindly.

Walk the line one character at a time with an `inQuotes` flag. A `"` toggles quote state — except when you're already inside quotes and see two `""` in a row, which is the CSV escape for a literal quote character (consume both characters, emit one `"` into the current field, and stay in quoted state). A comma only ends the current field when `inQuotes` is false; inside quotes, it's just a character to append.

Time: O(n) in the length of the line, one pass. Space: O(n) for the output fields. For production use, reach for a maintained library (e.g. CsvHelper) rather than this — real-world CSV also has to handle quoted fields containing embedded newlines, which a single-line parser like this one doesn't attempt.
scenario: A data-ingestion pipeline at a logistics company hit silent data corruption when a naive `Split(',')` parser split a customer name like "Smith, John" into the wrong number of fields; replacing it with exactly this quote-aware, character-by-character parser fixed the ingestion without needing a heavier CSV library.

problem: Given a large log file where each line has a timestamp and a level (e.g. `2024-01-01T10:15:32Z ERROR Payment failed`), implement a function that counts log entries per hour, per level — without loading the entire file into memory at once.
solution:
The "without loading it all into memory" constraint is really about the caller's choice of input, not just the aggregation logic: accept an `IEnumerable<string>` and iterate it with a plain `foreach`, so the function itself never materializes a list of all lines. The caller then passes something lazy — `File.ReadLines(path)`, which yields one line at a time as the file is read — rather than `File.ReadAllLines(path)`, which reads the whole file into an array up front. The aggregation function is identical either way; only the caller's choice determines whether the whole pipeline actually streams.

For each line, parse the timestamp and level, truncate the timestamp down to the hour (zeroing out minutes/seconds), and use that `(hour, level)` pair as a dictionary key to accumulate a running count. The working set is bounded by the number of distinct hour-level buckets, not by the number of log lines — for a service running steadily, that's a small, roughly constant number even as the log file itself grows into gigabytes.

Time: O(n) in the number of log lines, single pass. Space: O(distinct hour-level buckets), typically orders of magnitude smaller than the input.
scenario: An observability team built exactly this streaming, IEnumerable-based log aggregator to compute hourly error-rate buckets over gigabyte-sized log files on a machine with limited memory, deliberately avoiding `File.ReadAllLines` so the working set stayed bounded by the number of hour-level buckets, not file size.

problem: Design and implement the core logic of a URL shortener: given a long URL, produce a short, unique code, and resolve that code back to the original URL. Explain why generating a random short string and hoping it's unique doesn't scale well, and what the more robust alternative looks like.
solution:
Generating a random code and then checking the datastore for a collision works, but the collision probability rises as the number of stored URLs grows (a birthday-paradox problem), so at scale you end up doing more and more retry round-trips to the datastore just to find a free code. The more robust approach sidesteps collisions entirely: assign every new URL a unique, auto-incrementing integer ID (a database identity column/sequence gives you this for free, already safe under concurrent inserts), then base62-encode that ID into a short string (using `0-9A-Za-z`, 62 symbols). Two different URLs always get two different IDs, so two different short codes — no collision check needed at all.

Resolving is just the inverse: base62-decode the short code back into the integer ID, then look up the original URL by that ID. Base62 (rather than base64) is a deliberate choice for URLs — it avoids `+`, `/`, and `=`, which need escaping in a URL path.

Time: O(log₆₂ id) to encode or decode — effectively a small constant for any realistic ID range (a 6-character code already covers over 56 billion IDs). Space: O(1) per shortened URL, beyond the underlying storage of the mapping itself. Note the `_nextId++` shown here is for illustration only — a real implementation needs an atomic ID source (a DB sequence, not an in-process counter) to stay correct under concurrent requests across multiple server instances.
scenario: A marketing-tech company's URL shortener used exactly this auto-incrementing-ID-plus-base62 approach after an earlier random-code version started hitting frequent collisions as the link table grew past tens of millions of entries, each collision costing an extra round-trip to check and retry.

problem: One customer's integration retries every failed call immediately and without backoff. During a brief blip in a downstream dependency, that single customer's retry storm multiplied their normal traffic by 15x, pushed your shared API past capacity, and made requests time out for every other customer on the same cluster — even though their own traffic never changed. The postmortem asks: how do you stop one bad actor from being able to do this again, and how do you roll the fix out without the fix itself causing an outage?
solution:
The root cause is that one client's misbehavior wasn't isolated from anyone else's traffic, so the fix is per-client rate limiting at the API gateway — cap each API key/tenant to its own quota (token bucket, so short bursts are still fine) instead of only having a single global capacity limit that anyone can exhaust. Return `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header so well-behaved clients back off correctly, and log/alert on clients that get limited often so it surfaces as a signal, not just a silent rejection.

That alone doesn't fully fix it: if the limiter state is only in-process and the API runs on multiple instances, a client can still blow past the intended limit by fanning out across instances, so the counter needs to live in a shared store like Redis with an atomic increment-and-expire per window. It's also worth fixing the actual trigger, not just the symptom — reach out to the offending customer about adding exponential backoff with jitter to their client, since a rate limit alone doesn't make their retries succeed any faster, it just contains the blast radius.

For the rollout, don't flip enforcement on for every client at once — ship the limiter in shadow/log-only mode first (record who *would* have been throttled and by how much) so you can see real traffic against real thresholds before anything gets rejected, then enable enforcement for a small percentage of tenants or the specific offending client first, watch error rates, and widen from there. Turning on hard enforcement globally on day one, with limits guessed rather than measured, risks throttling legitimate customers and manufacturing the exact kind of outage you're trying to prevent.
scenario: At an API platform company, one customer's un-backed-off retry logic during a brief downstream blip multiplied their traffic 15x and took down the shared cluster for every other customer; the team added per-client rate limiting backed by Redis so the limit held across all instances, shipped it in shadow mode first to see real thresholds, and only then enabled hard enforcement starting with the offending client.

problem: Leadership wants every merge to `main` to reach production with no one manually clicking "deploy" — but they are nervous a bad change could reach customers unnoticed if the pipeline is too permissive. Design a CI/CD pipeline that automatically builds a container image from a code change and deploys it to production, but only after passing several independent automated gates. What are those gates, in what order, and how does the image actually travel from a git push to a running container in prod with no human in the loop?
solution:
Full automation to prod is safe only if each stage is a hard, independent gate that can stop the pipeline on its own — the safety comes from the layering, not from any single check. A reasonable order: (1) build and run unit tests — fastest feedback, fails cheaply; (2) static analysis and a dependency/SAST vulnerability scan on the source; (3) build the container image once, tag it immutably with the commit SHA, and push it to a registry — every later stage promotes this exact same image, it's never rebuilt; (4) scan that built image itself for OS/package vulnerabilities (e.g. Trivy) before it's allowed to be deployed anywhere; (5) deploy the image to a staging environment automatically and run integration/end-to-end tests against it; (6) only if every prior gate passed, deploy to production progressively — a canary or blue-green rollout to a small slice of traffic first, with automated health checks (error rate, latency) deciding whether to proceed; if those metrics breach a threshold, the pipeline auto-rolls back to the previous image tag without waiting for a human to notice.

The reason this is safe without a manual approval step is that no single gate is trusted alone: a security hole that slips past the SAST scan should still get caught by the image scan; a logic bug that passes unit tests should get caught by integration tests in staging; and a bug that somehow passes everything is still contained to a small percentage of prod traffic by the canary before it's ever fully rolled out, with rollback itself automated rather than depending on someone watching a dashboard. Each stage only promotes the one immutable image built in step 3 — nothing is ever rebuilt from source directly into production, which is what guarantees that what was tested is exactly byte-for-byte what's running.

# .github/workflows/deploy.yml -- simplified multi-gate pipeline
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: dotnet test                       # gate 1: unit tests
      - run: dotnet-sonarscanner begin && dotnet build && dotnet-sonarscanner end  # gate 2: static analysis

  build-image:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: docker build -t registry.internal/app:${{ github.sha }} .
      - run: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH registry.internal/app:${{ github.sha }}  # gate 3: image scan
      - run: docker push registry.internal/app:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build-image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: kubectl set image deployment/app app=registry.internal/app:${{ github.sha }} -n staging
      - run: ./run-e2e-tests.sh https://staging.internal      # gate 4: integration/e2e tests

  deploy-prod-canary:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: kubectl set image deployment/app app=registry.internal/app:${{ github.sha }} -n prod-canary
      - run: ./watch-metrics.sh --window 5m --max-error-rate 1%  # gate 5: automated health gate
        # non-zero exit here triggers the rollback job below instead of promote-full

  promote-full:
    needs: deploy-prod-canary
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: kubectl set image deployment/app app=registry.internal/app:${{ github.sha }} -n prod  # 100% rollout, same image, no rebuild

problem: Your team currently provisions AWS resources by clicking through the console, and undocumented manual changes have caused two outages this quarter because nobody could tell what the environment was actually supposed to look like. You're asked to bring the estate — a mix of EC2 instances, an ECS cluster running containerized services, and several Lambda functions — under Infrastructure as Code. Design the approach: which tool(s) do you use for what, how do you avoid Terraform and CloudFormation fighting over the same resources, and how does a change actually get from a pull request to applied infrastructure?
solution:
Standardize on one tool as the source of truth for a given resource rather than mixing Terraform and CloudFormation over the same infrastructure — having both able to manage, say, the same ECS service means whichever one runs last silently reverts the other's change, which reintroduces the exact "nobody knows the real state" problem you're trying to fix. Terraform is the more common default for a mixed EC2/ECS/Lambda estate since it's cloud-agnostic, has a large module ecosystem, and treats all three services uniformly rather than requiring AWS-native tooling like SAM only for Lambda; CloudFormation is a reasonable choice instead if the team is AWS-only and wants first-party support with no external state backend to manage — the deciding factor is team familiarity and whether multi-cloud is ever on the roadmap, not that one is objectively superior.

Structure the code as reusable modules per concern (networking, ECS service, Lambda function) rather than one monolithic template, store Terraform's state remotely in S3 with a DynamoDB table for state locking (so two engineers or two pipeline runs can't corrupt state by applying concurrently), and never let engineers apply from their laptops — every change goes through a PR, and CI runs `terraform plan` on the PR itself so reviewers see the actual diff of real infrastructure before approving, then `terraform apply` runs automatically (or with a single required approval gate for production specifically) only after merge. Run a scheduled `terraform plan` against every environment on a cron (e.g. nightly) purely to detect drift — anyone who still edits something by hand in the console shows up as an unexpected diff instead of silent, undocumented state, which is exactly the failure mode that caused the two outages.

scenario: At a retail company that had caused two outages from undocumented console changes, the platform team standardized on Terraform with S3 remote state and DynamoDB locking, required every change through a PR with `terraform plan` visible to reviewers, and caught the next manual console edit as an unexpected drift diff in a nightly scheduled plan instead of a third outage.

problem: On-call engineers currently triage CloudWatch alarms by tabbing between the AWS console, pasting log excerpts into a chat with an AI assistant, and manually correlating timestamps across several log groups — 15-20 minutes of legwork before actual root-causing even starts. You're asked to wire Claude Code directly into CloudWatch so it can pull the relevant alarm, metrics, and logs itself during an incident. What do you set up, and what guardrails do you put around it given that this hands an AI agent direct read access to production monitoring data?
solution:
The setup itself is straightforward: install `uv` on the on-call engineer's machine (or bake it into a shared incident-response image so every on-call engineer has an identical, tested environment), then register AWS Labs' `cloudwatch-mcp-server` as an MCP server in Claude Code's config. Verify `uvx awslabs.cloudwatch-mcp-server@latest` actually starts on its own before wiring it in — a broken subprocess just silently fails to expose any tools rather than throwing a clear error, which is the last thing you want to discover mid-incident.

The part that actually needs design thought is the guardrails, because the real security boundary here is the IAM role the server runs as, not anything about the agent's behavior. Point it at a dedicated, read-only profile scoped to exactly `cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms`, `logs:FilterLogEvents`, `logs:GetLogEvents`, and similar read actions — never a broad admin or write-capable role — so the agent has no path to acknowledge an alarm, delete a log group, or change an alarm threshold on its own initiative. Scope that role's resource policy to the specific log groups and namespaces on-call actually needs, not the whole account, so a confused or hallucinating session has a small blast radius instead of visibility into every system's logs. And treat every query the same way you'd treat someone pasting log data into a doc: it's still subject to whatever compliance/data-handling rules apply to what's in those logs (PII in log lines, etc.), so audit CloudTrail for that role periodically rather than assuming "it's just an AI reading it" changes the obligation.

Finally, decide up front how far to trust its output: it's genuinely good at accelerating correlation — which alarm fired, what else moved in the surrounding metrics and logs, candidate root causes — but keep a human as the one deciding the actual remediation action, at least until the team has enough track record with it to know how reliable its analysis is under real incident pressure.
scenario: At a SaaS company, on-call engineers spent 15-20 minutes manually correlating CloudWatch alarms across log groups before root-causing anything; wiring Claude Code into a read-only CloudWatch MCP server scoped to only the on-call log groups (no write or alarm-mutation permissions) cut that correlation time to under two minutes while keeping a human as the one deciding the actual remediation.
